extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers in algebraic/topological topology studying CW complexes, ENRs, and the compact-open topology
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and propositions about CW complexes, ENRs, compact-open topology, simplicial and sΔ-complex structures, and related homotopy properties. Includes proofs, corollaries, and exercises relevant to algebraic topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem A.7: ENR characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact subspace K of R^n is a retract of some neighborhood iff K is locally contractible in the weak sense that for each x ∈ K and each neighborhood U of x in K there exists a neighborhood V ⊂ U of x such that the inclusion V → U is nullhomotopic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: If K is a retract of some neighborhood, then it is a retract of every smaller neighborhood (so neighborhoods may be taken open or not). The proof constructs a CW structure on R^n − K with cells shrinking near K, then inductively builds a subcomplex Z and map r: Z→K and extends r by identity on K to a continuous retraction on Z ∪ K which contains a neighborhood of K. The converse uses that retracts of locally contractible spaces are locally contractible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Euclidean Neighborhood Retract (ENR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A space X is an ENR if for some n there exists an embedding i: X ↪ R^n such that i(X) is a retract of some neighborhood in R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: For compact X the existence of a retraction is independent of embedding choice. ENR property is used in Lefschetz fixed point theorem and Alexander duality contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary A.8: ENR ⇔ retract of finite simplicial complex
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact space is an ENR iff it can be embedded as a retract of a finite simplicial complex. Hence the homology groups and the fundamental group of a compact ENR are finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: finite simplicial complexes embed in R^n and hence are retracts of neighborhoods; conversely, a compact K retracting from an open U ⊂ R^n can be captured by a finite simplicial subcomplex of a sufficiently fine barycentric subdivision whose simplices lie within U and which retracts to K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary A.9: Compact manifolds are ENRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every compact manifold, with or without boundary, is an ENR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: Manifolds are locally contractible. For compact manifolds produce an embedding into some R^k by collapsing complements of finitely many coordinate balls to points and embedding the product of spheres; compactness ensures the composite is an embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary A.10: Finite CW complexes are ENRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every finite CW complex is an ENR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on number of cells; show finite CW complex can embed in some R^n by embedding subcomplex and attaching cells using explicit coordinate constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'Dominated by' a space
rubrics_metrics.description: A space Y is said to be dominated by a space X if there are maps Y → X → Y whose composite r∘i is homotopic to the identity on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: domination is a homotopy-theoretic weakening of retract, depending only on homotopy types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.11: Domination by CW ⇒ homotopy equiv. to CW
rubrics_metrics.description: A space dominated by a CW complex is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mapping telescope constructions T(f1,f2,...) and basic facts: (1) telescopes of homotopic maps are homotopy equivalent, (2) T(f1,f2,...) ≃ T(f2,f3,...), and (3) T(f1,f2,...) ≃ T(f2f1,f4f3,...). Then assembling telescope of i,r gives Y up to homotopy and also realizes it as a CW complex telescope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary A.12: Compact manifolds have CW homotopy type
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact manifold is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from manifolds being dominated by finite CW complexes (Corollary A.9 and Proposition A.11). Note: further refinements about existence of CW or simplicial structures depend on dimension; simplicial structures exist for dimensions ≤3, counterexamples exist in higher dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping telescope facts (used in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary facts about the mapping telescope T(f1,f2,...): (1) T(f1,f2,...) ≃ T(g1,g2,...) if fi ≃ gi for each i. (2) T(f1,f2,...) ≃ T(f2,f3,...). (3) T(f1,f2,...) ≃ T(f2f1,f4f3,...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are used to rearrange/combine telescopes and reduce to telescopes of cellular maps, enabling CW-type conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: compact-open topology subbasis
rubrics_metrics.description: For the mapping space X^Y, a subbasis consists of sets M(K,U) = {f: Y→X | f(K) ⊂ U} where K ⊂ Y is compact and U ⊂ X is open. A basis consists of finite intersections of such sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Y is compact, neighborhoods of f are controlled by finite partitions of Y into compact sets mapping into open neighborhoods of f(Ki). For paths (Y=I) basis neighborhoods correspond to partitions of I into closed intervals and prescribing open neighborhoods of the image on each interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.13: compact-open = uniform topology (metric) under hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a metric space and Y is compact, then the compact-open topology on X^Y equals the metric topology defined by d(f,g) = sup_{y∈Y} d(f(y),g(y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof shows each epsilon-ball contains a compact-open neighborhood and conversely each subbasic M(K,U) contains an epsilon-ball around f with epsilon being the distance from f(K) to complement of U. Use finite covers since f(Y) compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.14: evaluation and adjointness continuity properties
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The evaluation map e: X^Y × Y → X, e(f,y)=f(y), is continuous if Y is locally compact. (b) If f: Y×Z → X is continuous then the associated map f^: Z→X^Y, f^(z)(y)=f(y,z), is continuous. (c) The converse to (b) holds when Y is locally compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provide the adjoint relationship used in homotopy theory: continuity of maps Y×Z→X corresponds to continuity Z→X^Y under local compactness hypotheses. Part (a) is used to deduce (c). Local compactness of Y is emphasized repeatedly as necessary for these equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of Proposition A.14
rubrics_metrics.description: Various consequences: continuity adjunctions justify identification of path/homotopy spaces; image-in-subspace criteria for maps into mapping spaces; and more technical constructions used later (products/quotients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete use: basepoint-preserving homotopies correspond to maps into subspaces of mapping spaces; compactness/local-compactness hypotheses ensure expected adjunctions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.15: product topology compactly generated under hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a compactly generated Hausdorff space and Y is locally compact, then the product topology on X × Y is compactly generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces continuity checks to compact subsets and uses that on compact sets the product and product-with-compactly-generated-topology agree. Uses Proposition A.14(b),(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.16: natural homeomorphism for mapping-spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The map X^Y × Z → (X^Y)^Z, f ↦ (z ↦ (y ↦ f(y,z))) is a homeomorphism if Y is locally compact Hausdorff and Z is Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: exhibit subbasis correspondence M(A×B,U) ↔ M(B, M(A,U)) and use normality/compactness arguments to reduce general subbasic sets to these forms; local compactness and Hausdorff hypotheses are used for normality and product-compact arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.17: quotient map stability under product with locally compact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: X→Y is a quotient map then f × id: X × Z → Y × Z is a quotient map whenever Z is locally compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Proposition A.14 to related adjoint maps and continuity of identity; commonly used when Z = I to deduce that homotopies defined on quotient spaces are continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.18: Homotopy Extension Property (HEP) ⇔ retraction property
rubrics_metrics.description: A pair (X,A) has the homotopy extension property iff X × {0} ∪ A× I is a retract of X × I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: one direction easy; the other (without assuming A closed) uses a retraction r: X×I → Y = X×{0} ∪ A×I and shows openness criteria for subsets of Y determined by their intersections with X and A×I, leading to existence of required extensions. Example given showing the necessity of hypotheses (counterexample where retraction does not exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and distinctions: ordered Δ-complex, unordered Δ-complex, regular CW
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered Δ-complex: a CW complex where each n-cell has a distinguished characteristic map σ_α: Δ^n → X inducing an ordering on vertices of every face. Unordered Δ-complex: same but faces' characteristic maps are specified only up to symmetries permuting vertices. A CW complex is regular if characteristic maps can be chosen as embeddings so closed cells are homeomorphic to closed balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: unordered Δ-complexes (generalized triangulations) can be barycentrically subdivided to yield ordered complexes; unordered structures worse for products. Regular CW complexes are homeomorphic to simplicial complexes after suitable subdivisions; barycentric subdivision twice yields a simplicial complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: sΔ-complex (singular Δ-complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: A singular Δ-complex is a CW complex with distinguished characteristic maps σα: Δ^n → X whose restrictions to faces are compositions σα|_{face} = σ_β ◦ q for q a linear surjection taking vertices to vertices (preserving order). This allows attaching via arbitrary simplicial maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: sΔ-complexes permit quotient constructions, mapping cylinders, cones, and attachments by simplicial maps (not only cellular maps), solving shortcomings of ordinary Δ-complexes for quotients and attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial description: simplicial sets and geometric realization
rubrics_metrics.description: A simplicial set is a contravariant functor from the category Δ* (objects ordered sets [n], morphisms order-preserving maps including surjections) to Sets. For any simplicial set Y the geometric realization |Y| = (⊔_n (Y_n × Δ^n))/~ where identifications come from action of face/degeneracy maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition A.19: Every simplicial set is isomorphic to one of the form sΔ(X) for some sΔ-complex X (unique up to isomorphism). Degenerate simplices and uniqueness-of-degeneration statements are discussed and used to construct the sΔ-complex from a simplicial set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A.19: simplicial sets ↔ sΔ-complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simplicial set Y is isomorphic to one of the form sΔ(X) for some sΔ-complex X, unique up to isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: analyze degenerate vs nondegenerate simplices in Y, show uniqueness of representations, and reconstruct an sΔ-complex whose geometric realization is the expected |Y|. Observes simplicial sets are in general large but have a geometric sΔ-core.
